title: Trump Imposes 'Forced Labor' Tariffs on 60 Nations as Global Levy Expires
excerpt: New duties of 10% to 12.5% cover virtually all U.S. imports under Section 301, replacing the temporary global surcharge at the exact moment it lapsed.
body:
• Section 301 tariffs hit 60 economies covering 99.4% of U.S. imports, with 12.5% on 38 nations including China and 10% on 17 including India.
  • The duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT Friday, the same moment Trump's temporary 10% global tariff expired after 150 days.
  • Exemptions cover oil, gas, fertilizer, foodstuffs, aircraft parts, critical minerals, and goods already under Section 232 duties.
  • Two U.S. small businesses filed a lawsuit hours after the tariffs took effect, calling them an overreach of presidential authority.

The Trump administration on Friday imposed new tariffs of 10% and 12.5% on goods from 60 trading partners — covering 99.4% of all U.S. imports — alleging those nations had failed to curb imports made with forced labor. The duties took effect at 12:01 a.m. EDT, the precise moment a temporary 10% global surcharge expired after its legally mandated 150-day window.

The action represents the White House's most ambitious effort yet to rebuild President Donald Trump's near-global tariff wall after the U.S. Supreme Court in February struck down his "reciprocal" duties of 10% to 50%, which had been imposed under the International Emergency Economic Powers Act (IEEPA) in April 2025.

How the New Tariff Structure Works

The Office of the U.S. Trade Representative imposed the duties under Section 301 of the Trade Act of 1974 — a legal mechanism that has survived prior court challenges, making it a safer bet than the IEEPA authority the Supreme Court rejected.

Thirty-eight economies, including China, Brazil, Russia, Vietnam, and Australia, face the higher 12.5% rate. Another 17 — among them India, Canada, Mexico, the United Kingdom, Indonesia, and Pakistan — drew the lower 10% rate, which the administration says reflects their existing bans or plans to ban forced labor imports.

For five additional partners — the European Union, Japan, South Korea, Switzerland, and Taiwan — the duty tops up to 10% or 12.5% rather than stacking on top of existing rates. That structure honors bilateral deal commitments the administration had made with those economies.

"The United States has had a forced labor import ban for nearly a century, and rigorously enforces it. It's well past time for our trading partners to do the same."

— Jamieson Greer, U.S. Trade Representative

Extensive Exemptions Soften the Blow

The tariffs come with a long list of product carve-outs that mirror administration priorities: oil and gas, fertilizer, certain foodstuffs, aircraft and parts, critical minerals, and anything already carrying Section 232 national security duties on autos, steel, aluminum, or copper. The USTR added 471 products to the exclusion list in the final order.

The Budget Lab at Yale estimated that the average statutory U.S. tariff rate stood at 12.1% as of July 21. With the new duties running, that figure is projected to reach 12.8% by year-end — costing the average American household roughly $1,100 annually. Had the temporary tariff lapsed without replacement, the rate would have fallen to 9.8%, with an estimated cost of about $550 per household.

Global Reactions: Anger, Resignation, and Relief

Trade partners reacted with a mix of outrage and pragmatism. China said it opposed all unilateral tariffs, adding that trade wars served no one. Australia and Brazil called the duties unjustified and pledged to seek their removal. Norway said there was "no basis" for them.

The European Union struck a more measured tone, noting the outcome aligned with the U.S. tariff commitments agreed under their joint statement. A European Commission spokesperson said the arrangement provided "positive momentum" for further negotiations.

Britain reported no negative change for its businesses. The UK's 10% rate holds alongside separately negotiated sectoral deals on steel, pharmaceuticals, and whisky. The first tariff-free shipment of Scotch whisky under a deal clinched during King Charles's visit to Washington was expected to depart by week's end.

"I think this is more status quo in terms of the economic impact."

— Kelly Ann Shaw, former White House trade adviser, partner at Akin Gump

Legal Challenge Already Filed

Hours after the tariffs took effect, two U.S. small businesses filed suit in the U.S. Court of International Trade in New York, backed by the same nonprofit legal group that successfully challenged earlier rounds of Trump tariffs before the Supreme Court.

The plaintiffs argue that Section 301 tariffs have historically been targeted at specific nations and industries, and that applying them as a near-universal blanket levy has no historical precedent. They also contend the administration is attempting to re-impose duties that the Supreme Court already deemed illegal.

Unlike previous legal challenges that succeeded, however, Section 301 carries a stronger legal track record. The law has been used regularly by past presidents, giving the administration a more defensible foundation — though the breadth of this action remains untested.

What It Means for India

India drew the lower 10% tariff rate, credited with having laws that ban forced labor imports. But Indian exporters face a separate risk: a second Section 301 investigation into excess manufacturing capacity remains open against 16 trading partners, including India, the EU, China, Japan, South Korea, and Switzerland. That probe could layer additional duties onto the forced labor tariffs already in effect.

For Indian-American business owners importing goods from India, the 10% rate offers some relief relative to the 12.5% hitting Chinese and Vietnamese suppliers. The exemptions on critical minerals and certain foodstuffs may also benefit importers in the spice and agricultural commodity sectors.

What Comes Next

The forced labor tariffs are only the first phase of the administration's post-Supreme Court trade strategy. The excess capacity investigation targeting 16 partners could yield additional duties in the coming months. Canada faces a separate 50% tariff on a broad range of goods set to take effect in August.

Markets reacted with relative calm on Friday, with bond yields edging higher on inflation risk but equities more focused on the ongoing U.S.-Iran military conflict. The Dow, S&P 500, and Nasdaq ended the session mixed. For now, the tariffs represent a familiar status quo — but the legal and diplomatic battles are just getting started.
nri_angle: India faces the lower 10% tariff rate for having forced labor import bans, but a second Section 301 probe into excess manufacturing capacity could add more duties, while Indian-American importers benefit from exemptions on critical minerals and foodstuffs.
